# Restored clocks through the GPU reload

Status: in use (CRIU `--timens-no-wait`, gpushare `--clock-at`, agent). Scope: the agent (`restore_clock.go`, `restore_v2.go`, `restore_span_learned.go`), CRIU's `--timens-budget`, and
`nvsnap-gpu-suspend resume`.

## 1. The problem

A restored task's clocks are meant to continue from the values its dump recorded, so a task that was
waiting on a timeout when it was dumped does not find it expired. `--timens-budget` does this for CRIU:
the restored clocks start that far behind the dumped values, and CRIU resumes the tasks only once their
CLOCK_MONOTONIC has reached them (`timens_wait_dumped_clocks`). The agent sizes the budget from this
checkpoint's last CRIU restore on the node (`restore_clock.go`).

With gpushare, CRIU's restore is not the end. The workload's processes stay held after CRIU while
`nvsnap-gpu-suspend` loads their GPU memory, remaps the fabric handles and resumes them. All that time,
their clocks run. In a 2-node restore of a 2-node engine (Kimi-K3, 2 nodes with 4x GB300 each, 2026-10-24, nvsnap build
and driver not recorded; [the record](../results/KIMI-K3-RESTORE-2026-10-24.md), section 1):

| Step | Time |
|---|---|
| CRIU restore done, budget 7 s | 00:03:31 |
| GPU memory loaded, handles exchanged, remapped | 00:03:31 → 00:05:08 |
| `resume hold`: the processes run | 00:05:08 |

Each restored process saw about 90 s go by at once (vLLM logged
`No available shared memory broadcast block found in 60 seconds` as it resumed), so anything with a shorter
timeout fires at once. NCCL's RAS thread, for one, declares a peer dead after 60 s without contact
(`RAS_PEER_DEAD_TIMEOUT`); in one restore that path crashed a rank (an NCCL 2.30.7 use-after-free in
`rasMsgHandlePeersUpdate`, reported to NCCL separately) and failed the restore. The clock jump is ours to
fix.

## 2. What has to hold

At the moment the restored tasks run again, their CLOCK_MONOTONIC reads the dumped value, plus at most a
small overrun. No task ever reads a value earlier than one it read before the dump.

All the tasks of a restore share one time namespace, so they share one offset. So every task has to be
held until the clocks reach the dumped value, including any process gpushare does not hold today (a
follower's health server, for one), not only the GPU processes.

## 3. Proposal

**Budget.** The budget covers the whole restore up to the resume: CRIU, the GPU memory load, remap and
resume. The agent records that span after each restore (from CRIU's start to `resume hold`), not only
CRIU's, and uses it with the same margin next time. Before a checkpoint's first restore it estimates the
span from the CRIU images and the GPU memory to load.

**The wait moves to the resume.** CRIU starts the clocks behind by the budget but does not wait itself. If
it did, a budget of about 100 s would hold back the GPU load, which needs the tasks restored, and add those
100 s to every restore. Instead, just before the resume, the tasks wait until their clocks reach the
dumped values. That wait is where `nvsnap-gpu-suspend resume` releases them: it can read the restored
clock the way CRIU's `timens_wait_dumped_clocks` does (the time namespace's offsets and the dumped value
from the `timens` image).

A restore faster than its budget waits the difference at the resume, before the tasks run. A slower one
leaves the overrun counted, as CRIU's budget does today. The recorded span makes the next one right.

**Learned span.** The estimate's rates and slack were set on the slowest cluster seen, where a 2-node
Kimi-K3 rank's GPU load and resume took about 97 s after CRIU (the 2026-10-24 restore above, its record
section 1). Another cluster restored a 2-node Kimi-K3.1 rank (826 GB of GPU memory; 2 nodes with 4x GB300
each, driver 610, 2026-11-14, nvsnap agent v0.2.91-rc8) in 33 s, then waited out the estimate's 130 s at
the resume: its instance took 153 s, about 95 s of it waiting (the agent's restore phase histograms and the
two rank nodes' `restore-span-ms` files; [the record](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/nvcf/issues/3490)). Every
first restore of a capture, and every restore on a node new to it, pays that.

So a first restore of a checkpoint on a node also adds its span, with its checkpoint's size, to the
ConfigMap `nvsnap-restore-spans` in the agent's namespace, keeping the 8 newest of its shape: its GPU
product and the number of members of its group (a multi-node instance's fabric remap is a fixed cost a
pod on its own does not have). A restore with no span of its own on its node takes, before the estimate,
the largest of its shape's spans, each scaled up to its checkpoint's size when that is larger (never
down), plus a fifth for being another checkpoint's, then the usual margin. That budget is never more than
the checkpoint's estimate: a learned span only shortens the wait, and a cluster with no restore of that
shape keeps the estimate. For the rank above, on a node new to it after its first restore elsewhere,
that is about 50 s instead of 130 s, computed from its numbers by `TestLearnedSpanBudgetKimi`. Measured
on a 4-node Kimi-K3 instance (4 nodes with 4x GB300 each, 2026-11-15, nvsnap agent v0.2.91-rc15; [the
record](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/nvcf/pull/3491), its Verification section): a first restore with no
sample waited about 68 s for its clocks under the estimate's 1m53s budget; the next, on a node new to the
checkpoint, took the learned span (54.5 s, a 1m5s budget) and waited about 15 s. The ConfigMap is per cluster, so each cluster learns its own nodes
and fabric. A group restore's driver works the span out once, from its largest rank, and never below a
rank's own last span; each rank bounds it by its own estimate, which for ranks of one instance is about
the same (`internal/agent/restore_span_learned.go`). Samples come only from first restores on a node,
the restores that use them, and are written in the background, so a slow API server does not hold a
rank's report. The span file is the node's own: the checkpoint manifest leaves it out, and a fetch over any
tier (the rails, a shared filesystem, a peer) drops it when done, so a node that fetched the checkpoint is
still new to it. Should a checkpoint take longer than its learned span, the overrun is counted by the
restored clocks; the margin keeps that well under RAS's 60 s for a checkpoint like those of its shape,
and its own span then makes its next restore right. Sizes are whole checkpoints, so a checkpoint whose
size is mostly files rather than GPU memory scales less well; the estimate bounds the long side only.
The restore phase `clock_wait` (part of `gpu`) shows the time each rank waited.

**One budget for a group's ranks.** The GPU ranks of a group restore start CRIU together and resume when
their clocks reach the dump, so a rank's budget decides when it resumes. The recorded span is per node and
per checkpoint, and an instance's ranks are not always placed on the nodes that restored them before. With
budgets of their own, a rank new to its node waits out the estimate while the others resume on their last
span. The others then run with their network locked until the last rank restores. In a 4-node Kimi-K3
restore, one rank took the estimate, much longer than the others' last span. The others waited locked
until it resumed, and the leader's workload exited before the unlock, which failed the restore.

So the driver reads each rank's recorded span from its node's agent (`restore-span-ms`, through the
checkpoint file endpoint) and hands every rank the same one in the restore request (`groupRestoreSpanMs`):
the largest. When a rank has none, the driver takes the cluster's learned span for the shape of its
largest rank instead, raised to any rank's own span that is larger (a known span that wins is not marked
learned), and each rank bounds a learned one by its estimate; only with no learned span either is it -1,
for which every rank takes the estimate. Companions keep their own budget, which covers CRIU only.

| Part | Change | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| CRIU (our fork) | a restore option that applies `--timens-budget` without waiting; used with `--leave-stopped` | nvsnap |
| `nvsnap-gpu-suspend resume` | `--clock-at <ns>`: wait until the restored clock reaches `<ns>` before the thaw | gpushare |
| agent | record and use the whole span as the budget; read `<ns>` from the `timens` image; resume CRIU's listed tasks after `resume` | nvsnap |

## 4. Agreed with gpushare

- **What `resume` releases.** Only the pids it is given: the GPU processes `stop` left SIGSTOPped, which
  CRIU dumps and restores stopped. It ptrace-freezes every thread of those pids except the driver's
  restore thread and gpushare's control thread, sends SIGCONT, and keeps them frozen through load, remap
  and resume. Every other task CRIU restored (the multiprocessing resource tracker, a health server) runs
  as soon as CRIU finishes. So gpushare alone cannot hold the whole tree.
- **So CRIU restores the whole tree stopped** (`--leave-stopped`, `final_state = TASK_STOPPED`), and
  applies the budget without waiting. `timens_wait_dumped_clocks` runs before the detach whatever the
  final state, so a no-wait option combines with `--leave-stopped` cleanly. That still has to be tested.
- **`nvsnap-gpu-suspend resume --clock-at <ns>`.** Before it thaws the GPU processes, the tool waits until
  the restored CLOCK_MONOTONIC reaches `<ns>`. It reads the restored clock as its own CLOCK_MONOTONIC,
  minus its own time namespace's monotonic offset, plus the one in `/proc/<pid>/timens_offsets` of a
  restored pid, as CRIU's `timens_wait_dumped_clocks` does. It does not enter the time namespace.
- **`<ns>` comes from the agent.** It decodes the checkpoint's `timens` image (`crit decode`, as it
  already does for `pstree.img`). The image holds the dumped namespace's CLOCK_MONOTONIC and
  CLOCK_BOOTTIME at the moment the tasks were seized (`timens_note_seized`), not at the end of the dump.
  The wait uses CLOCK_MONOTONIC; BOOTTIME moves with it.
- **After `resume` returns,** the agent resumes the other tasks. CRIU writes the pids of the tasks that
  ran at the dump to `timens-resume-pids` in its work directory (`-W`, the placeholder's writable work volume) before it stops them all, so a task
  that was stopped at the dump stays stopped. The agent finds the listed pids in CRIU's pid namespace
  and sends each SIGCONT, leaving out the GPU processes, which `resume` thawed. No task then runs
  before the clocks reach the dumped values.
- **The agent uses this only when both halves are there:** the bundled CRIU lists `--timens-no-wait`
  and the bundled `nvsnap-gpu-suspend` lists `--clock-at` in its usage. Otherwise CRIU's own budget
  applies, as before.
- **The `open` reply timeout** is done (gpushare 38fa2235f): `open` goes to every pid at once, each with
  at most 10 s to reply.

**To watch in the first run:**

- The driver's restore thread and gpushare's control thread run during load and remap while the
  clock is behind the dumped value. The control thread uses CLOCK_REALTIME only, which is not
  namespaced. Whether the driver's restore thread has a CLOCK_MONOTONIC timeout that a clock behind the
  dump could trip is not known.
- With `--hold-gate`, the CPU side runs from the thaw and only GPU launches wait for `open`. That gap
  (about 6 s here) still counts as run time, well under RAS's 60 s.

## 5. Tests

- **Agent:** the budget is the recorded whole span with its margin, falls back to the estimate, and is
  bounded. The span is recorded only for a restore that resumed.
- **Agent, group restore:** every GPU rank gets the slowest rank's span; when any rank has none or its
  span does not parse, the learned span (below), else the estimate; companions get none (`TestGroupRestore_OneClockSpanForTheRanks`,
  `TestGroupRestoreSpanBudget`).
- **Agent, learned span:** recorded per shape (GPU product and group size), newest 8 kept, conflicts
  retried; the largest scaled up, never down, with its margin, and never past the estimate; none from
  another shape; a group's ranks get it from the largest rank and never below a rank's own span
  (`TestLearnedSpan`, `TestRecordAndReadLearnedSpan`, `TestRecordLearnedSpanRetriesConflicts`,
  `TestLearnedGroupSpan`, `TestGroupRestoreSpanBudget`, `TestGroupRestore_LearnedSpanForANewRank`).
  A node's span file stays its own: the manifest leaves it out, a peer fetch skips it, also from an
  older peer that lists it, and a done fetch over any tier drops it
  (`TestCheckpointManifest_LeavesOutNodeLocalRecords`, `TestEnsureLocal_PeerFetchSkipsNodeLocalRecords`,
  `TestLocalFetch_DoneFetchDropsTheSourceNodesSpan`).
- **CRIU:** with the new option, the restored clock starts behind by the budget and CRIU returns without
  waiting.
- **On the cluster:** a Kimi-K3 2-node restore logs no `No available shared memory broadcast block`
  after the resume. A small probe in the workload that reads CLOCK_MONOTONIC before the dump and after
  the restore sees the gap within the budget's margin.
